title: It’s full of stars!
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6723, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: It may look like snow falling on a winter's night, but this is NGC 6723, a globular cluster in Sagittarius, seen in infrared light, taken with ESO's VISTA telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Globular clusters are spherical groups of stars bound tightly by gravity. The name comes from the Latin globulus, small sphere, which undersells clusters like NGC 6723 that hold hundreds of thousands to millions of stars. Astronomers have found more than 150 in the Milky Way, most thought to be 10 billion years old or more and hosting some of the galaxy's oldest stars.

These clusters also helped us find our place in the galaxy. Early in the 20th century, the American astronomer Harlow Shapley worked out how far away several of them were, and noticed they formed a roughly spherical spread with the Sun off-center. He correctly concluded that the Milky Way's heart lies at the center of that spread, putting the Sun in the galactic suburbs.
scale: NGC 6723 lies about 28 000 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.

understand.summary: VISTA's VIRCAM camera imaged the cluster in near-infrared light through J, H and Ks filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
